title: Attempt budgets on repair edges
description:
`Repair -> lint -> Repair` spins forever otherwise, burning tokens on a loop
nobody is watching.

## Acceptance criteria

- Attempt count is edge state carried in the token, not something the agent
  tracks in its own context.
- Budget is per-edge and declared in the graph definition. Default 3.
- Exhaustion routes to a human node — an edge, not an exception.
- A test proves a repair cycle terminates.

title: beads in faceoff-finder
description:
Only ai-ih-coach has a real backlog today: 55 issues, 51 dependency edges
(18 blocks, 32 parent-child, 1 related), longest chain 7 deep, zero dangling
references. That is a well-formed DAG.

faceoff-finder's work lives in a 47KB `FINDINGS.md` prose file. Prose is not
dispatchable — the runner moves tokens, and a token is an issue with acceptance
criteria. Until this exists, faceoff-finder cannot enter the graph at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- `.beads/` initialized and committed, with a prefix.
- `FINDINGS.md` triaged into issues that have acceptance criteria. The file
  either shrinks to a genuine findings log or is retired.
- `br ready` returns work a Builder node could actually start.
- Dependencies set, so ready means ready.
notes:
When this lands, three issues move out of control-plane's backlog with it. They
are labelled moves-to-faceoff-finder and blocked on this issue, and
tools/check-backlog-scope.py turns the gate RED the moment
faceoff-finder/.beads/issues.jsonl exists — the exemption is self-expiring on
purpose, so the move cannot be deferred quietly:

  cp-golden-set-games-a2f       which games form the golden set
  cp-golden-set-harness-f2g     the harness that scores them
  cp-lint-ratchet-identity-7or  tools/lint_ratchet.py lives in faceoff-finder

Two couplings to handle in the same change, or the gate stays red for the wrong
reason:

1. GRAPH.md cites a2f and f2g by id, and tools/check-issue-refs.py fails on an id
   that no longer exists in this backlog. Either update those citations to the
   new faceoff-finder ids, or teach check-issue-refs to resolve ids across
   factories. The second is probably right — control-plane legitimately talks
   about work that lives elsewhere, and it will do so again.
2. The control-plane concern behind the golden set does NOT move: faceoff-finder's
   autonomy stays capped until its gate means something. That belongs here, as a
   graph fact about which nodes are human-occupied. Keep an issue for it, pointing
   at the faceoff-finder ones.

title: beads in finance-c-and-c
description:
Same as faceoff-finder, sourced from `plans/*.md`.

Lower priority only because this factory has a mandatory human node before merge,
so an unformed backlog costs less here — nothing lands unsupervised regardless.

## Acceptance criteria

- `.beads/` initialized and committed.
- `plans/*.md` triaged into issues with acceptance criteria.
- `br ready` is meaningful.

title: Builder node
description:
## Acceptance criteria

- Takes one ready beads issue, does the work, returns a typed result carrying the
  file list and a commit chunking plan.
- Runs `./verify --fast` in its inner loop — that tier exists for exactly this —
  but does not get to decide whether it is done.
- Cannot merge, cannot close the issue, cannot cross its own outgoing edge.
- Runs `bin/verify-all` and checks the exit code as an explicit step. It must not
  rely on the pre-push hook having fired: `SKIP_VERIFY=1` and `--no-verify` both
  bypass it, so the hook is advisory against a determined process and is not the
  gate.

The Builder needs *a* backlog to take work from, not faceoff-finder's specifically — control-plane and ai-ih-coach both have real ones, and the first live run targets control-plane. faceoff-finder still needs its backlog before it can enter the graph at all, which is what that issue is for.

title: Draft CHARTER.md for ai-ih-coach
description:
Draft from `README.md`, which this repo's own CLAUDE.md calls "the design
document, not just a setup guide" — so most of the charter already exists in
prose and needs extracting rather than inventing.

## Acceptance criteria

- Draft exists, short, with a real out-of-scope list.
- Proposes a single north-star metric.
- Reviewed and corrected by Nikita.

title: Draft CHARTER.md for faceoff-finder
description:
Draft from `README.md` and the 47KB `FINDINGS.md`, for Nikita to correct.

The north-star metric is the hard part and the part that matters: this repo runs
at roughly five times the commit rate of the other two, which is either the
engine working or scope with no floor under it. The charter is what tells those
apart.

## Acceptance criteria

- Draft exists, is short, and names an out-of-scope list with real entries.
- Proposes a single north-star metric and says what it deliberately ignores.
- Reviewed and corrected by Nikita before anything depends on it.

title: Draft CHARTER.md for finance-c-and-c
description:
Draft from `plans/*.md` plus `data/northstar.yaml` and `src/northstar.ts`, which
already encode a north star in code — the charter should agree with them or
explain why it does not.

Must state the standing constraint plainly: this factory never auto-merges. Real
money, real tax lots, real wash-sale windows. A mandatory human node sits before
merge and its removal is not on the table.

## Acceptance criteria

- Draft exists and agrees with `data/northstar.yaml`, or documents the divergence.
- States the no-auto-merge constraint and why.
- Reviewed and corrected by Nikita.

title: CHARTER.md in each factory
description:
The root node of each factory's work graph. Owned by Nikita — agents may file a
charter question against a charter, never edit one.

Without it the Reviewer has nothing to judge "should this exist at all" against,
and `cp brief` has nothing to summarize toward. A charter question is also the
only legitimate way for an agent to push back on scope, which is what keeps
scope drift visible instead of silent.

## Acceptance criteria

- All three exist. Each states what the company is, its north-star metric, and
  what is explicitly out of scope.
- Each is referenced from that factory's CLAUDE.md.
- None ships without Nikita's correction — drafted here, owned there.

title: cp status / cp brief — the seat
description:
Read-only across all four repos.

The payoff of the whole design lands here: the decision queue is exactly the set
of tokens parked on human nodes. That makes "surfaces decisions, never diffs"
mechanical instead of aspirational — and makes its violation detectable.

## Acceptance criteria

- `cp status`: per factory — gate state, ready count, WIP, tokens parked on human
  nodes.
- `cp brief`: what changed since the last read, and what needs Nikita.
- If a diff reaches Nikita without having sat on a human node first, that is a
  missing edge. The panel says so, and it gets filed as a bug in the panel.
- Read-only. It cannot advance a token. Anything that advances a token is the
  runner's job.

title: No-edge-matched is a visible terminal, not an exception
description:
If no edge matches the verdict, the token stops and reports. An LLM router would
have improvised past the gap and hidden it; this makes the missing edge findable.
Deadlock here is a feature and should be kept as one.

## Acceptance criteria

- An unmatched verdict parks the token on a human node, carrying the reason.
- It appears in the decision queue like any other parked token.
- A test removes an edge from the graph definition and asserts the token parks,
  rather than crashing or proceeding.

title: Edge contract: deterministic transition scripts
description:
What an edge is allowed to be, written down before there are many of them.

## Acceptance criteria

- An edge is a script. Its exit code selects the outgoing branch. It is a pure
  function of (node result, repo state at a known commit).
- Exit code conventions align with the `./verify` contract already in use:
  0 proceed, 1 the check failed, 2 the edge itself is broken. 2 is never allowed
  to look like 1.
- Edges may carry state across crossings — attempt counts, the lint baseline —
  but that state lives on disk and in git, never in an agent's context.
- Replay: given a recorded node result and a repo at a known commit, crossing the
  same edge twice selects the same branch. A test demonstrates it.
- No edge invokes a model. A test greps the edge scripts for model invocation and
  fails if it finds one.
close_reason:
Built: bin/edges/_lib.sh (the contract as code every edge sources), `exits`
declared per edge in nodes/graph.json, tools/check-edges.py wired into ./verify,
CP_RESULT / CP_BASE / CP_WORKTREE supplied by the runner, and tests/test_edges.py
(14 tests).

All acceptance criteria met:
- An edge is a script; its exit code selects the branch. Three verbs — edge_ok,
  edge_failed, edge_broken — so there is one idea of what an exit code means
  rather than one per script.
- 0/1/2 aligned with ./verify, and 2 never looks like 1: different code AND
  different output ("BROKEN"), and check-edges fails the gate if an edge that can
  return both routes them to the same place. A missing input is edge_broken, not
  edge_failed — the reverse would route a missing input to a repair node that
  cannot fix it.
- Edge state stays on disk and in git; the attempt count already lived in the
  token rather than in any agent's context.
- Replay: a test crosses every non-factory edge twice with identical input and
  asserts the same branch, and that the exit it returned is one the graph routes.
- No edge invokes a model, checked over the files by tools/check-edges.py as well
  as the existing test.

Beyond the criteria, because the alternative was a contract with a hole in it:
edges are told their input (CP_RESULT, CP_BASE) rather than discovering it. An
edge that resolved HEAD itself would be a different function on every crossing,
which makes "pure function of (node result, repo at a known commit)" untrue in
the one way that matters — replay would prove nothing about the run it replays.

Found and fixed while writing the checker: scanning only the scripts graph.json
names would have skipped bin/edges/_lib.sh, which every edge sources. A model
call there is a model call on every edge, and it is precisely the file a
reference-following check does not look at. All files under bin/edges/ are
scanned now, and a test plants a probe in both positions.

Exit-2 routing destinations remain cp-verify-exit2-destination-3e5's; this issue
declares and checks the exits, it does not decide where they go.

title: Real edge scripts: commit, merge, close
description:
`bin/edges/commit`, `merge` and `close` echo a line and exit 0. The runner walks
straight through them, which is why every dry run looks so clean — nothing has
ever touched a repo.

Nothing tracked this until now, which is the more interesting fact: the graph was
built, validated, tested and rendered on top of four scripts that do nothing, and
the gate went green the whole time. A green board over stubs is exactly the
failure the golden set exists to prevent in faceoff-finder, one level up.

This is the least interesting and most load-bearing item left. It is where a bug
stops being a wrong number on a screen and starts being a wrong commit in a repo.

## Acceptance criteria

- `commit` stages exactly the files in the Builder's chunking plan and makes one
  commit per entry, with that entry's message. It refuses to commit a path the
  plan did not name — the plan is the contract, and a node that touched more than
  it declared is a finding, not something to tidy up silently.
- `merge` and `close` operate on the real branch and the real tracker.
- Each is a pure function of (node result, repo at a known commit): given the
  same plan and the same starting sha, it produces the same result. A test
  demonstrates it.
- None of them invokes a model. The existing test over `bin/edges/` must keep
  passing.
- Exit codes follow the house contract: 0 proceed, 1 the work failed, 2 the edge
  itself is broken. 2 must never look like 1.
- A dry run must remain incapable of touching a repo. Today `cp-run` swaps in
  `noop` for factory-scoped edges; whatever replaces that has to be at least as
  hard to get wrong.
close_reason:
Built: real bin/edges/commit, merge and close; `mutates` declared in graph.json
with exits [0,1,2] and distinct routes; edge_no_dry_run in _lib.sh; the runner's
dry-run guard rekeyed from cwd to `mutates`; tests/test_edge_scripts.py (18 tests)
against throwaway git repos and a throwaway beads workspace, never a factory.

All acceptance criteria met:
- commit stages exactly the paths the plan names, one commit per entry with that
  entry's message, and refuses if the worktree changed anything undeclared —
  exit 1, routed to repair, because committing the extra file would make every
  later claim about what a change contains untrue.
- merge and close operate on the real branch and the real tracker. Both use the
  cwd the runner sets rather than reconstructing /mnt/projects/<factory>, so
  there is one opinion about where a factory is instead of two.
- Pure function of (plan, base): a test builds the same repo twice, runs the same
  plan, and asserts the same tree sha. Commit shas carry a timestamp; the content
  that lands is what has to match.
- No edge invokes a model; check-edges.py and both existing tests still pass.
- 0/1/2 with 2 never looking like 1. Missing worktree, unknown base, unreadable
  plan, absent tracker are all edge_broken — sending any of them to a repair node
  produces an agent confidently editing code that was never the problem.
- A dry run is now incapable of touching a repo via two independent locks: the
  runner substitutes a no-op for any edge declared `mutates`, and each mutating
  script refuses again on CP_DRY_RUN. That is harder to get wrong than what it
  replaced, which keyed off the edge's working directory — covering the stubs by
  accident and about to stop covering them.

Three real bugs, none of which could have shown up while the edges were stubs:
- `tr '\x1e'` does not interpret the escape (tr wants octal, or bash's $'...').
  The declared-paths set was silently empty, so every actual change looked
  undeclared and no commit would ever have been made.
- `br show --json` returns a LIST, not an object. close read it as an object,
  got an empty status, and reported a real issue as missing — parking every
  token at the last hop before done.
- A token routed to a human terminal by an EDGE got status "human" and no
  question, so the decision queue never contained it. That is the panel's
  founding rule failing in the panel's own clothes. Fixed here because merge and
  close made the route reachable; filed as cp-routed-park-invisible-htf because
  it predates this change.

Also filed: cp-node-worktrees-do1. commit has to run where the Builder worked and
nothing creates that worktree yet, which is now the honest blocker in front of a
live run rather than a missing piece nobody had named.

title: Reviewer evidence is read from a well-known path, not from its own crossing
description:
The Reviewer's manifest carries `evidence` as a path plus a content hash, and the
runner fills it from `<factory>/verify-report.json` — whichever run happened to
write that file last.

Nothing ties it to *this token's* `verify-fast` crossing. A concurrent run in the
same factory, a hand-run `./verify --evidence`, or a stale file from yesterday all
produce a manifest that validates, hashes cleanly, and hands the Reviewer evidence
about a different tree. The hash makes the substitution auditable after the fact,
which is worth something, but it does not prevent it — the manifest records what
the node was given, and what it was given was wrong.

Found while building the manifest contract (cp-node-isolation-i7d). Filed rather
than fixed there because the fix is about how an edge hands its output to the next
node, not about what a manifest may contain.

## Acceptance criteria

- The evidence a node receives is the evidence its own gate crossing produced —
  keyed to the token and the run, not read from a well-known path.
- The `verify-fast` / `verify-full` edges write their evidence somewhere the
  runner can attribute to that crossing, and the transition log records which.
- A test: two tokens in the same factory, interleaved, each get their own
  evidence. Today that test would fail.
- A manifest whose evidence cannot be attributed to a crossing is refused rather
  than assembled — an unattributable input is not better than a missing one.

title: The execution graph: judgment in nodes, transitions in scripts
description:
The frame the other issues are built into.

Nodes are where judgment happens — agent work, nondeterministic. Edges are
transitions implemented as deterministic scripts. The rule that makes it worth
anything: **a node has no way to advance except across an edge.** An agent
cannot decide it is done, cannot route itself, cannot skip ahead.

This is LangGraph's shape with the LLM router removed. The router is the worst
possible place for nondeterminism: once a model chooses transitions, the
reachable states of the system stop being enumerable, and nothing downstream can
be reasoned about. With scripted edges the state space is finite and drawable,
which buys resumability, auditability, testability, and author-never-judge as a
structural property rather than an instruction in a prompt.

**Scope of this backlog.** This tracker holds *program* work — the operating
model across all four repos: the graph, its contracts and runtime, the gate
machinery, and the autonomy ceiling. Feature work for a factory belongs in that
factory's own backlog. The line: if it changes how work moves, it lives here; if
it changes what the product does, it lives there.

title: Structured file list on issues — the work-to-code edge
description:
33 of 55 ai-ih-coach issues name a file path — `shared/capture.ts`,
`server/src/pose.ts`, `experiments/render_pose.py` — but only inside free-text
descriptions. There is no structured field joining an issue to code.

So the work graph and the code graph are two disconnected components, bridged
only by an agent reading prose and grepping. That costs twice: the join is
re-derived on every run, and the Reviewer cannot mechanically check that a diff
touched what the issue said it would.

## Acceptance criteria

- Issues carry a structured file list. Decide between labels, a metadata field,
  or a naming convention, and write down why.
- Backfilled for the 33 ai-ih-coach issues that already name paths in prose.
- The Reviewer node can compare "files the issue claimed" against "files the diff
  touched" with no model involved.
- A referenced path that no longer exists is reported, not silently ignored —
  stale edges are the named failure mode of this whole approach.

title: First live run: one token, end to end, on control-plane
description:
The point at which this stops being a document.

Everything demonstrated so far runs on recorded verdicts. The graph mechanics —
routing, budgets, parking, resume, provenance — are real and tested. **The
judgment is fake.** This issue is where we find out whether a Builder node under
a tool policy can produce a diff worth reviewing, which no amount of dry-run
proves.

**Target: control-plane itself, on a small issue.** Deliberately boring.

- Lowest blast radius — it is tooling, not the hockey pipeline and not the
  portfolio.
- Fastest gate in the fleet, a couple of seconds full.
- If the Builder writes rubbish, `./verify` catches it and nothing operational is
  lost.

**Not ai-ih-coach**, which has live migration work in flight; an agent committing
into that is a conflict someone untangles by hand.

**Put a human node in front of `merge` for every factory for run one** — the
finance setting, temporarily, everywhere. `graph.json` already supports it:
add `"human_before": ["merge"]` to each factory. Take it back out per factory
only on evidence, which is what `cp-golden-set-games-a2f` gates for
faceoff-finder and what Stage 5 was always about.

## What success is

Narrow, and not "the agent did good work":

- A token enters, a real diff comes out, `./verify` goes green on it.
- The Reviewer approves without ever having seen the Builder's transcript, and a
  test proves the input set rather than the prompt asking nicely.
- It parks on the human node. Nikita clicks merge in the panel.
- The journey list shows every step, and the manifest hash on each crossing
  answers "was isolation held".

**The machinery held.** That is the whole bar for run one.

## Blocked on

`cp-node-isolation-i7d`, `cp-node-tool-policy-wyi`, the real edge scripts, and
the Reviewer then the Builder. Dropping the live-mode refusal in `bin/cp-run` is
the **last** line changed, never the first.

title: Decide the canonical games for the faceoff-finder golden set
description:
**Blocked on Nikita. This is not the pipeline's decision to make.**

faceoff-finder's chosen autonomy level is auto-merge-on-green. But green there
currently means only "it imports and it lints". Nothing checks that faceoff
detection, clock reading or jersey identity are *right*, and all three can
degrade without raising a single exception — the current way that gets noticed is
watching a bad short go out days later. Until the golden set exists, the chosen
autonomy level for this factory is not safe.

`games/` holds 37 directories: 27 dated, 10 legacy-named. Candidates that map
onto failure modes which have actually bitten:

- **2026_08_13_juggernaughty_vs_ice_monkeys** — the game named in the
  `_display_format` docstring, where the tenths-vs-M:SS ambiguity took the trace
  off the real clock at 1:00.2 in P3 and lost a buzzer-beater. Covers the clock
  failure mode directly.
- **gray** — the game the jersey-identity spike was validated on: 85% raw / 90%
  snapped number reading, 1255 raw traces resolving to 19 skaters. Covers jersey
  identity.
- Still needed: one with a truncated LiveBarn pull, and one with colour-similar
  jerseys.

Criteria, from `docs/verify-findings.md`: already labeled and trusted; varied
enough to cover the failure modes that have actually bitten; and stable — a
golden clip that gets re-ingested is not golden.

## Acceptance criteria

- Three or four games chosen, recorded on this issue.
- Each one's ingest is frozen, with "frozen" defined mechanically rather than by
  intent.
- The harness spec in `docs/verify-findings.md` is unblocked.

title: faceoff-finder golden set harness
description:
Builds what `docs/verify-findings.md` already specifies. Everything currently
gated checks that the code *runs*; this is the first check that it is *right*.

Unit tests are the wrong instrument for a CV pipeline. The right one is a fixed
handful of clips with committed expected outputs, scored against baselines with
tolerances, so a regression shows up as a red gate instead of as a bad short.

    tests/golden/
      cases/2026_08_13_juggernaughty_p3.json
      baselines/2026_08_13_juggernaughty_p3.json

## Acceptance criteria

- Each case names a game, a time span, and expected outputs: faceoff timestamps
  within a stated frame tolerance, the reconstructed clock at K sample points,
  jersey identity for the players in frame.
- The runner scores actual against expected and fails when a metric drops below
  its committed floor.
- Wired into the full tier of `./verify` and into the nightly sweep.
- Could never have run anywhere but here — the footage lives in `games/`, not in
  the repo. This is the concrete reason the no-CI decision was right.

title: Declarative graph definition format
description:
One file that enumerates the graph, so it can be validated and drawn instead of
being reconstructed by reading code.

Deliberately not LangGraph: a framework would be taken on to get conditional
edges we would write anyway, and every node shells out to `claude -p` regardless.
A declarative file plus a small runner is a couple hundred lines and stays
inspectable, which is the whole point.

## Acceptance criteria

- One file listing nodes, edges, and which actor may occupy each node
  (`agent` | `human`).
- Per-factory overrides: finance-c-and-c inserts a human node before merge;
  faceoff-finder and ai-ih-coach do not.
- A validator: every edge's source and target exist, every node is reachable
  from the entry, and every terminal is either `merge` or a human node.
- Attempt budgets are declared here, not hardcoded in the runner.

comments.text:
Built and tested in dry-run, but NOT closed: beads refused because this has open blockers, and it is right to. I built these ahead of the edge contract and on a runner that cannot yet launch live nodes, so 'done' here means 'done for dry-run'. Leaving the dependency honest rather than forcing the close.

What exists now: nodes/graph.json, tools/check-graph.py in ./verify, bin/cp-run walking it, and tests/test_run.py covering the behaviour this issue asks for. Closing follows the blockers.

title: Write GRAPH.md — the execution graph model
description:
The artifact that makes the graph inspectable. Today the transitions exist but
are scattered: some in `.githooks/pre-push`, some in CLAUDE.md prose, and the
rest in whoever happens to be driving. Nothing enumerates the nodes and edges,
so nothing can check the graph for holes.

Must cover:

- Node vs edge, and the rule that the model never routes.
- Why the router is the worst place for nondeterminism — with scripted edges the
  reachable state space is finite and enumerable.
- The typed verdict contract, and why parsing prose in an edge smuggles the
  nondeterminism straight back into the router as a regex pretending to be a
  state machine.
- Edges are deterministic *as a function of their input*, not absolutely.
  Functional core, imperative shell: the commit chunking plan is judgment, and
  executing it is not.
- A node's interior may be as freely agentic as it likes. The discipline governs
  transitions between committed units of work, nothing else.
- Where human nodes sit per factory, and the definition that falls out of it:
  **autonomy level = which nodes on the path are human-occupied.** "Merge on
  green except finance" stops being a policy sentence and becomes a graph fact.
- Failure terminals: no-edge-matched (deadlock, visible on purpose) and budget
  exhausted.
- How this layers with the work graph and with provenance. A beads issue is the
  payload that travels the edges; the transition log *is* the provenance record
  and needs no separate store.

## Acceptance criteria

- `GRAPH.md` at the control-plane root.
- Contains the node/edge diagram for the common path, plus the finance-c-and-c
  variant with its mandatory human node before merge.
- Names every piece already acting as an edge today: `./verify` (exit 0/1/2),
  `bin/verify-all`, `.githooks/pre-push`, `tools/lint_ratchet.py`.
- States explicitly what is NOT in the model yet, so the gap is readable rather
  than inferred.
- Describes no implementation that does not have an issue filed against it.
close_reason: GRAPH.md written and committed. All five acceptance criteria met: diagram plus the finance-c-and-c variant, every existing edge named, an explicit not-yet list, and no forward claim without an issue behind it (20 refs, all resolve).

title: Groomer node
description:
Turns intent into dispatchable work. The node that makes acceptance-criteria-
before-code mandatory instead of aspirational.

## Acceptance criteria

- Produces issues whose acceptance criteria are written before any code exists.
- Refuses to groom work with no charter line to hang from, and files a charter
  question instead of guessing.
- Sets dependencies, so `br ready` means ready rather than merely open.

title: cp-guard splits on shell operators inside quoted strings, and reshaped a verdict
description:
Found by running a real Reviewer node end to end under the policy
(cp-node-tool-policy-wyi). Two defects in bin/cp-guard's command matching, one of
them serious.

**1. Shell separators are matched inside quoted strings.** `segments()` regex-splits
the raw command text on `|`, `&`, `;`, backtick and `$(`. Those characters are not
operators when quoted. The Reviewer's own verdict payload described the bug it had
found — a `&` that should be `|` — and the guard split the JSON payload on the
characters inside the quoted summary, refusing the call.

The node then reworded the finding until it got through, emitting "Union used where
intersection is needed" instead of the literal expression. So the guard silently
shaped the content of a Reviewer's verdict. A control that quietly edits what a
judge is able to say is worse than one that fails loudly, and this failure mode is
invisible from the outside: the verdict validated, the token advanced, and the only
trace was four denials in the log that read like the node misbehaving.

**2. Every segment must match the SAME pattern.** `matches()` uses
`all(prefix_matches(s, prefix) for s in segs)`, so `git show X | head` is refused
even though both halves are innocuous, because `head` does not start with
`git show`. A command should be allowed when every segment matches SOME allowed
pattern.

Both were caught by the same live run that confirmed the hook fires at all. Neither
was reachable from the offline tests, which only ever passed single commands.

## Acceptance criteria

- Splitting respects quoting. A separator inside single or double quotes is data.
  Use a real lexer rather than a regex over raw text.
- Unquoted command substitution (`$(...)`, backticks) is still denied, and so is
  substitution inside double quotes, where it still executes.
- A compound command is allowed when every segment matches some allowed pattern,
  and denied when any segment touches a denied one.
- A curated set of read-only text filters (head, tail, wc, sort, uniq, cut, nl,
  cat) is available to nodes that read, so normal work does not require the model
  to work around the guard. sed, awk, perl, python, xargs and tee stay denied —
  they write or execute.
- A test with a payload containing `|`, `&`, `;` and `$(` inside quotes, asserting
  it is allowed, plus the escalation cases asserting they are not.
- A test that an unparseable command is denied rather than passed.
close_reason:
Fixed in bin/cp-guard: segments() now uses shlex in non-POSIX mode so quotes
survive on tokens, with a separate raw scan (tracking single-quote state) for
command substitution, since tokenising can split `$(` into `$` and `(` and lose
the signal. Matching changed from "every segment matches the SAME pattern" to
"every segment matches SOME allowed pattern", and an unparseable command is
denied rather than guessed at.

Also granted read-only filters (head, tail, wc, sort, uniq, cut, nl, cat, column,
grep) to every node, and explicitly denied the writers and interpreters beside
them (sed, awk, perl, python, ruby, node, xargs, tee, dd, install, chmod, curl,
wget, nc, ssh). Without the readers, ordinary work required working around the
guard — which is exactly what the bug looked like from the outside.

Verified by re-running the same live Reviewer against the same diff. Before the
fix its verdict avoided the literal characters and read "Union used where
intersection is needed". After, it says `not (seen | terms)` and `if not
(seen & terms):` — the expressions it could not previously emit — and it found a
second finding as well. Six new tests in tests/test_policy.py cover the quoted
payload, per-segment matching, the writer denials, and unparseable input.

The general lesson is the expensive one: this was invisible to the offline tests
because they only ever passed single commands, and invisible in production
because the node adapted. A control that a model routes around leaves a passing
gate and a quietly worse verdict.

title: Audit the ambient leak channels between nodes
description:
Blocking the transcript is the easy part. The channels that actually leak are
ambient, and none of them are currently closed:

| Channel | Leak |
|---|---|
| Working tree | Builder leaves scratch files or notes the Reviewer then reads |
| beads fields | Builder writes issue notes; the Reviewer reads the issue |
| The payload | a free-text field carries an argument for approval |
| `~/.claude` memory | Builder writes a memory; the Reviewer's session loads `MEMORY.md` |
| MCP servers | ambient capability present in every node |
| Commit messages | Builder writes prose aimed at the reviewer |
| Code comments | `// reviewer: this is intentional` |

The memory channel is specific to this setup and currently wide open:
`~/.claude/projects/-mnt-projects-control-plane/memory/` loads into every session
in this project, which is a direct unguarded path between any two nodes.

Two of these cannot be closed, only bounded. Commit messages are part of the diff
and cannot be withheld from a reviewer that needs to read the diff; the
mitigation is that they are treated as **claims to verify**, never as context to
trust. Reviewer-addressed code comments are the same — undetectable in principle,
but flaggable in practice.

## Acceptance criteria

- Reviewer runs against a clean worktree at the commit: tracked files at that
  sha, nothing else. Verified by a test that plants a scratch file and asserts it
  is not visible.
- Per-node memory directory, or memory disabled for nodes.
- Builder has no write access to the tracker.
- A planted-persuasion test: Builder leaves a note arguing for approval through
  each channel above; assert none reach the Reviewer's manifest.
- Channels that cannot be closed are documented as bounded, with what bounds them.
notes:
Measured 2026-08-21 while building the manifest contract (cp-node-isolation-i7d).
The audit should start from these rather than re-derive them:

- ~/.claude memory: a headless run INSIDE the project directory receives the
  operator's MEMORY.md *index* verbatim — one line per memory, Builder-authored
  free text. Memory *bodies* are NOT loaded (canary in a body returned NO). So
  the channel is narrow but real and points the wrong way.
- --system-prompt does not close it. --setting-sources "" does not close it.
- --bare does close it (skips auto-memory) but cannot authenticate on an OAuth
  subscription: "Not logged in · Please run /login". Redirecting
  CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR fails identically — credentials live there. Nodes run on
  Claude Code, not an API key, so --bare is out by decision, not circumstance.
- Changing cwd out of the project DOES close it: auto-memory is keyed by project
  path; a run elsewhere reported NONE.

Now enforced: cp-manifest check refuses a manifest whose cwd is inside the
project, and the runner puts every node in a worktree under /tmp/cp-worktrees.
Still open for this issue: working tree, beads fields, commit messages, code
comments, and whether a node can reach ~/.claude at all via Read.

title: Lint ratchet keys nodes by file path — a rename silently loosens the baseline
description:
`tools/lint-baseline.json` keys entries as `faceoff_finder/instagram/api.py::F401`.
Rename or move that file and the node identity breaks: its banked violations
disappear from the baseline instead of reappearing as regressions, so the ratchet
quietly gets looser and reports less debt than exists.

This is the textbook graph-engineering failure — entity identity, and stale edges
that make a wrong answer look structured. Worth fixing before anything else in
this backlog starts depending on path-keyed identity. 27 violations are banked
today.

## Acceptance criteria

- Renaming a file that has banked violations does not reduce the reported debt.
- Either the baseline is keyed by something stable, or `check` fails loudly when
  a baselined path no longer exists. Decide which, and write down why in
  `docs/verify-findings.md`.
- `python tools/lint_ratchet.py debt` output is unchanged for an untouched tree.
- A test covers the rename case.

title: Live per-node-type tool policy check, outside the gate
description:
cp-node-tool-policy-wyi asked for a test per node type that launches the node,
attempts a forbidden call, and asserts both that it was blocked and that it was
logged. What landed is the offline half: every node type's policy is asserted
through the guard's real decision function, and one live probe (reviewer,
attempting Edit) confirmed the PreToolUse hook fires, denies, and writes a
violation row.

The live half is deliberately not in `./verify`. The gate must run offline — it
cannot depend on a model being reachable, and a gate that needs the network is
not a gate on this machine. So the per-node-type live check needs somewhere else
to live.

Worth knowing before writing it: the reviewer probe did not attempt `Edit` at
all. It attempted `ToolSearch` to go and load `Edit`. A live test that asserts
"the forbidden tool was attempted and blocked" will assert on the wrong tool
name unless it accounts for that.

## Acceptance criteria

- A check, outside `./verify`, that launches each node type under its real
  policy, attempts a call that policy denies, and asserts the denial and the
  violation row.
- It is runnable on demand and its last result is visible, so "when did we last
  confirm the locks work" has an answer that is not "someone did it once".
- It does not run in the gate, and the gate does not pretend it did.

title: control-plane is not in the mirror set
description:
Stage 0 gave the three factories a bare mirror on the NVMe root disk, away from
the `sda1` that `/mnt/projects` lives on. control-plane was created after that
pass, so it has no mirror — and it holds the only copy of `bin/verify-all`, the
factory template and this backlog. It was not even a git repository until today.

## Acceptance criteria

- `~/git-mirrors/control-plane.git` exists.
- `~/git-mirrors/sync` includes it and reports its uncommitted count like the
  other three.
- One clean sync run reporting no uncommitted work.
close_reason:
~/git-mirrors/control-plane.git created, sync updated to cover all four repos, one clean run with no uncommitted work anywhere. Also pushed to github.com/nikita-leonov/control-plane, so this repo has two copies.

Recorded in the script header which repos have a GitHub remote and which do not, so the finance-c-and-c exception reads as deliberate rather than forgotten.

comments.author: nikital
comments.text: Pushed to git@github.com:nikita-leonov/control-plane.git (88a20a5) on 2026-08-21, so this is no longer the only copy. That covers off-machine durability; this issue is now specifically about the local NVMe mirror, which is the copy that survives GitHub being unreachable or the account being locked. Note the other three factories are NOT on GitHub — finance-c-and-c deliberately so.

title: Node isolation contract: what a node may see
description:
"The Reviewer never sees the Builder's transcript" is currently an intention with
nothing enforcing it. This makes it a property of the runner.

Isolation is a property of the *process*, not of the model. Each node is a
separate `claude -p` invocation with a fresh context window, so nodes cannot
share state — the only question is what bytes the runner puts in. A node
therefore never *inherits* context; it *receives a manifest* assembled by a
deterministic script. That is what makes isolation testable rather than hoped for.

Banned outright, in every node invocation: `--resume`, `--continue`,
`--fork-session`. Those are the literal inherit-the-transcript flags; a node that
resumes is not a node.

Required: `--system-prompt` (full replacement, never `--append-system-prompt` —
appending leaves the default agent prompt underneath with behaviours nobody
chose or audited), `--strict-mcp-config` (otherwise every ambient MCP server is
live inside every node; in this environment that is Gmail, Drive, Calendar and
Chrome, and a Reviewer that can send email is not a Reviewer),
`--disable-slash-commands`, and `--output-format json`.

## Acceptance criteria

- An input manifest format: the exact, enumerated set of inputs a node receives.
  Nothing outside the manifest can enter.
- The manifest is hashed and the hash recorded on the transition log, so "was
  isolation held" is answerable after the fact.
- The Reviewer's manifest is: the diff, the issue's acceptance criteria, the
  charter, and the verify evidence. Nothing else. A test asserts the exact set.
- The runner **strips** payload fields not in the manifest whitelist rather than
  forwarding them — otherwise a free-text field becomes a channel for the Builder
  to argue its case to the Reviewer.
- The banned flags are asserted absent by a test over the runner, not by
  convention.
close_reason:
Built: nodes/manifest.schema.json (the input manifest — the exact set a node
receives), per-node `inputs` whitelists and a `launch` block (banned/required
flags) in nodes/node-types.json, bin/cp-manifest (assemble | check | hash),
manifest assembly + hashing wired into bin/cp-run, and tests/test_manifest.py
(20 tests). tools/check-graph.py now gates the contract, so a node added without
a whitelist turns the board red rather than failing only in the suite.

All five acceptance criteria met:
- Manifest format enumerating each node's inputs; assembly is a whitelist copied
  OUT, never a blacklist deleted — a forgotten copy omits an input, a forgotten
  delete forwards one, and only one of those mistakes is safe.
- The manifest hash lands on the transition log at every crossing that leaves a
  node, so "was isolation held" is answerable from the log alone.
- The Reviewer's set is exactly {diff, criteria, charter, evidence}, asserted.
- Undeclared payload fields are stripped at assembly AND rejected at check, so a
  manifest built by anything else still cannot smuggle a field.
- Banned flags asserted absent over the runner's real argv, driven by the flag
  lists in node-types.json rather than strings copied into the test.

Two decisions beyond the criteria, both because the alternative was untested code:
- Manifests are assembled, validated and hashed on EVERY node visit including dry
  runs. Assembly that ran only live would be dormant until the one day it is
  load-bearing.
- build_launch_argv() is written and tested now, while live launch stays refused.
  A "banned flags are absent" test needs a real subject, and dropping the refusal
  later is now a one-line change rather than inventing the argv the same day.

The finding that changed the design: the memory channel was measured rather than
assumed. A headless run inside the project receives the operator's MEMORY.md
index verbatim (bodies are not loaded — a canary in a body returned NO). Neither
--system-prompt nor --setting-sources "" closes it. --bare does but cannot
authenticate on an OAuth subscription, and nodes run on Claude Code rather than
an API key, so it is out by decision. Changing cwd out of the project closes it.
So the closer is cwd, not a flag: it is a manifest field with a validator behind
it, and the runner puts every node in a worktree outside /mnt/projects.
GRAPH.md's "wide open ... loads into every session" is corrected to what was
measured. Filed cp-evidence-attribution-g5y for a real gap found on the way:
the Reviewer's evidence is read from a well-known path, not from its own crossing.

title: Per-node tool policy, deny by default
description:
Tools are limited per node, and the limits are enforced by the launcher rather
than requested in a prompt. `--allowedTools` is sub-tool scoped
(`Bash(git diff:*)` grants exactly that, not Bash), so the policy is real.

The two asymmetries that matter:

- **The Reviewer must not have Edit or Write.** A judge that can edit what it is
  judging is not a judge.
- **The Builder must not have `git merge`, `git push`, or `br close`.** It cannot
  cross its own outgoing edge — that is the rule the whole graph rests on, and
  here is where it stops being rhetorical.

## Acceptance criteria

- A declared allowlist per node type, living in the graph definition alongside
  the node, not scattered in launch scripts.
- Deny by default. A `PreToolUse` hook supplied via `--settings` is the backstop
  behind the allowlist, so a gap in one is not a gap in both.
- **An attempted violation is a signal, not just a denial** — it is recorded on
  the transition log and surfaced by the panel. A Reviewer that tried to call
  Edit is something to know about.
- A test per node type: launch it, attempt a forbidden call, assert both that it
  was blocked and that it was logged.
- Filesystem boundary via `--add-dir`, scoped to the node's worktree.
close_reason:
Built: per-node `tools` policy (allowed/denied) in nodes/node-types.json,
bin/cp-guard (hook | settings | check | policy), --allowedTools/--disallowedTools
and a generated --settings wired into cp-run's launch argv, violation rows on the
transition log, violations surfaced by both `cp status` and the web journey, four
new checks in tools/check-graph.py, and tests/test_policy.py (24 tests).

Criteria met:
- Allowlist declared per node type in the contract, not in launch scripts. The
  --settings file is GENERATED from that policy rather than kept beside it: two
  hand-maintained copies of one rule is two rules.
- Deny by default, with the PreToolUse hook as the backstop behind the allowlist.
  A guard launched without CP_NODE denies everything rather than guessing.
- A violation is a signal: it lands on the transition log with kind=violation,
  shows in `cp status` undimmed, and appears in the token's journey — never
  counted as a crossing, because it happened AT a vertex, not between two.
- Filesystem boundary via --add-dir scoped to the worktree.

Partially met, and filed rather than glossed: "a test per node type: launch it,
attempt a forbidden call". Every node type is asserted through the guard's real
decision function, and one live probe confirmed the hook fires, denies and logs.
The live per-node-type version cannot go in ./verify — the gate must run offline
— so it is cp-live-policy-check-tas.

Two things measurement added that the criteria did not ask for:
- Compound commands. A prefix match on Bash(git diff:*) would pass
  `git diff && rm -rf .`. Every segment is matched; an unparseable segment is
  denied rather than assumed harmless.
- The tools that grant tools. The live probe's Reviewer, told to edit a file,
  never attempted Edit — it attempted ToolSearch to go and load Edit.
  Deny-by-default caught it, but only because nobody had listed ToolSearch, and
  that safety evaporates the first careless widening. ToolSearch, Task and Agent
  are now explicit denials at every node plus a check in check-graph.py; Task and
  Agent because a node that spawns a subagent gets default tools, which is the
  whole policy bypassed in one call.

Also filed: cp-panel-escaping-v2b — violation text is escaped because a node
writes it, which leaves the rest of the panel inconsistently raw.

title: Nothing creates the per-token worktree that isolation and commit both assume
description:
Two things now depend on a per-token git worktree, and nothing creates one.

The isolation contract (cp-node-isolation-i7d) requires every node to run with
cwd outside the project directory, because auto-memory is keyed by project path
and a node run inside it receives the operator's memory index. `cp-manifest`
refuses a manifest whose cwd is inside the project, and `cp-run` computes
`/tmp/cp-worktrees/<factory>/<token>` — a path that does not exist.

The commit edge (cp-edge-scripts-zow) has to stage and commit the files the
Builder actually changed, which means it has to run where the Builder worked.

So the worktree is the shared assumption underneath both, and it is currently a
string rather than a directory.

## Acceptance criteria

- The runner creates a worktree per token, from the recorded base commit, on a
  branch named for the token — and removes it when the token reaches a terminal.
- It is outside the project directory. A worktree inside it silently reopens the
  memory channel, so this is checked rather than intended.
- Creation and removal are edges, or steps the runner records, so a token whose
  worktree could not be made stops visibly instead of running somewhere else.
- Re-running a token does not reuse a dirty worktree from a previous run.
- A test asserts the worktree path, that it is a real git worktree on the base
  commit, and that it is gone after the token finishes.

title: The panel escapes node-written text and nothing else
description:
`web/index.html` interpolates most values straight into `innerHTML`: issue
titles, token ids, question text and option labels among them. Those come from
the tracker and the runner rather than from a node, so the exposure is small
today — but the panel is the one surface in this system that changes anything,
and "small today" is a property of the current inputs, not of the code.

The violation rows added with cp-node-tool-policy-wyi are escaped, because the
tool call a node attempted is written by the node itself. That leaves the page
inconsistent: one field escaped, the rest not, which is worse than either
uniform choice because the next person reading it cannot tell which rule applies.

## Acceptance criteria

- One rule for the whole page: every interpolated value is escaped at the point
  of interpolation, or rendered with textContent.
- A test that a question, an issue title and a token id carrying markup render
  as text rather than as elements.
- The `esc()` helper's comment stops naming an exception, because there is none.

title: Panel: parked tokens and run history, once the graph runs
description:
The half of the panel that cannot exist until nodes actually run. Split out of
cp-cp-status-khe so the read-only board is not blocked behind the runtime.

Today "decisions" is approximated by issues labelled `blocked-on-nikita`, which
is a hand-maintained proxy. The real thing is the set of tokens parked on human
nodes, which is only meaningful once a runner is moving tokens.

## Acceptance criteria

- The decision queue is the actual set of parked tokens, and each renders its
  `question` — the asks line and its options — rather than a issue title.
- `cp why <token>` reconstructs the path a change took from the transition log,
  without reading an agent transcript.
- A diff that reached Nikita without having sat on a human node is reported as a
  missing edge, per GRAPH.md. That is the check that keeps "surfaces decisions,
  never diffs" honest.
- The `blocked-on-nikita` label proxy is removed once this lands, so there is one
  source of truth rather than two.

title: Reviewer node — built before the Builder
description:
Judge before author, and structurally rather than by instruction: the Reviewer is
a separate process that never sees the Builder's transcript. It reads the diff,
the issue's acceptance criteria, the charter, and the verify evidence. Nothing
else.

Built first on purpose. Scaling the author before the judge exists is how a
factory produces volume nobody can check.

## Acceptance criteria

- Returns `approve | reject | charter-question` plus findings. Never prose alone.
- Has no access to the Builder's transcript. A test asserts the exact input set.
- `charter-question` parks the token on a human node — that is the sanctioned way
  to push back on scope.
- Calibrated before it is given authority: run against a set of recorded diffs
  with known verdicts and check it agrees.

comments.author: nikital
comments.text: Correlated failure is the residual risk that isolation cannot touch. Process isolation buys information independence, not judgment independence — same weights, same priors, same blind spots, so a Reviewer on the same model tends to accept the flawed reasoning a Builder produced because it would have produced it too. Decide explicitly whether the Reviewer runs on a different model than the Builder, and record the reasoning. Bounds that do work regardless: the Reviewer's authority never overrides a deterministic check, and it is calibrated against recorded diffs with known verdicts before being granted any.

comments.author: nikital
comments.text: Unblocked from cp-files-edge-e4n on 2026-08-21. A structured file list makes the Reviewer's job cheaper — comparing what the issue claimed against what the diff touched without a model — but it is not a prerequisite: the Reviewer can read the diff. Blocking a first live run on a schema decision was my wiring, not a real dependency. cp-files-edge-e4n stays open on its own merits.

title: A token routed to a human terminal vanished from the decision queue
description:
A token that reaches `@park` by an edge ROUTE, rather than by a verdict that
parks, was given `status: "human"` (the terminal's `kind`) and no question. The
panel renders the decision queue from `status === 'parked' && t.question`, so
such a token appeared nowhere: not in the browser queue, not in `cp decisions`,
not in the sticky bar.

That is the panel's founding rule failing in the panel's own clothes — the
decision queue is supposed to be exactly the set of tokens parked on human
nodes, and this was a token parked on a human node that the queue did not
contain.

It had never fired because the only routes to `@park` were `verify-fast` and
`verify-full` exit 2, which no dry-run scenario produces. It became reachable in
normal operation with cp-edge-scripts-zow, where `merge` and `close` route
failures to a person.

Fixed there: arriving at a human terminal sets `status: "parked"` and synthesises
a question naming the edge and its exit code, so exit 1 and exit 2 read
differently to the person who has to act on them.

Filed because it was a real defect that existed before that change, and because
the shape of it is worth keeping: a route that nothing exercised behaved
differently from the path that everything exercised, and the tests all passed.

## Acceptance criteria

- A test that every terminal of kind `human`, reached by every route that leads
  to one, produces a token the decision queue actually contains.
- More generally: a check that no route target can produce a token which is
  neither running, done, nor visible as a decision.

title: The runner: cross edges, persist tokens, resume
description:
The thing that actually moves a token through the graph. Today nothing crosses
edges — a human does the next thing, which is exactly the bottleneck being
removed.

## Acceptance criteria

- Advances one token (one beads issue) until it reaches a terminal or parks on a
  human node.
- State persists on every crossing. `kill -9` mid-run and resume continues from
  the last crossing, not from the start.
- Never invokes a model to decide routing. This is the invariant the whole design
  rests on and it gets a test.
- `--dry-run` crosses the graph using recorded node results, with zero model
  calls, so the graph is testable without spending anything.
- Runs locally. No remote execution, per the standing decision.

comments.author: nikital
comments.text:
Framework evaluation, 2026-08-21: considered Mastra (mastra.ai) and declined. Its workflow engine matches five of our requirements (branch, typed step I/O, suspend/resume, durable snapshots, tracing), but it owns the LLM call by design — 'rather than requiring external process shells'. Our node is claude -p, a whole agentic harness, not a provider. Using its agents would mean rebuilding agentic coding on a raw model API; using it purely as a workflow engine would make every step an opaque subprocess while carrying agents, memory, RAG, evals and 90+ providers to get .branch().

Decisive point: it does not touch isolation (cp-node-isolation-i7d, cp-node-tool-policy-wyi, cp-leak-audit-z57), which is where our actual risk is.

Also: its suspend/resume solves a problem we do not have. It is built for a server surviving deployments and awaiting async callbacks. Our suspend is 'the process exits and a JSON file remains'; the human runs cp the next morning.

Revisit if any of these become true: the panel grows a real web dashboard with live runs; nodes need to wait on genuine async external callbacks; runs need to be multi-tenant or hosted; or hand-rolled resume proves buggy in practice.

comments.author: nikital
comments.text:
Half done, and the half that is done is the half that mattered to prove. bin/cp-run walks the graph, persists token state atomically on every crossing, resumes from a parked token carrying its own run mode, and never invokes a model to route — asserted by a test over the edge scripts, not just claimed.

Live node launch is deliberately refused: cp-run exits 1 with a pointer to cp-node-isolation-i7d and cp-node-tool-policy-wyi. Launching nodes with ambient tools and no manifest is the exact failure the graph exists to prevent, and a runner that quietly does it anyway is worse than one that will not start. So this stays open until isolation lands.

Dry-run works against scenario fixtures in tests/fixtures/, which is how the graph is testable with zero model calls.

title: Sweeper node
description:
The nightly local pass. Everything it runs is local, per the standing decision.

## Acceptance criteria

- Runs `bin/verify-all` at the full tier, the faceoff-finder golden set, a mirror
  sync, and a stale-branch report.
- Anything it finds becomes an issue, not a notification. A notification is
  something to ignore; an issue is something with a state.
- Reports to the panel and never opens a diff.

title: The mirror script is not itself mirrored
description:
`~/git-mirrors/sync` is the tool that makes every other repo durable, and it
lives in a plain directory in `$HOME`, tracked by nothing. The disk it protects
against losing is not the disk it sits on, so this is not urgent — but it is the
one file in the setup whose loss is silent, because nothing would report it
missing until the day it was needed.

It is fleet tooling, which is what this repo is for. `bin/verify-all` and it are
the same kind of thing.

## Acceptance criteria

- `sync` lives in `bin/` here and is under version control.
- The copy in `~/git-mirrors/` is a symlink, or removed in favour of invoking it
  from here — decide which and say why, since a symlink into `/mnt/projects` from
  the NVMe root reintroduces a dependency on the disk being mirrored away from.
- One clean run after the move.

title: Transition log — provenance as a byproduct
description:
If every transition is a script, the log of crossings *is* the provenance record.
"Why did this land" becomes a path through the graph rather than a 40k-token
transcript nobody will read. This is the difference between a CEO seat and
another inbox.

## Acceptance criteria

- Append-only NDJSON. One record per crossing: timestamp, token, from node, to
  node, edge, verdict, exit code, duration, commit.
- Reconstructs the full path of any merged change without reading an agent
  transcript.
- Committed to git — it is evidence, not a cache.
- Rotation policy decided and written down, not left to grow unbounded.

comments.author: nikital
comments.text:
state/transitions.ndjson exists and is written before the next crossing starts, with fsync — timestamp, token, factory, from, verdict, edge, exit, to, ms, and a why for the non-obvious hops. cp serve reads it, and selecting a token renders its whole path.

Two criteria are not met yet, which is why this stays open. It lives under state/, which is gitignored — the criterion says committed, because the log is evidence and not a cache. And there is no rotation policy. Both need deciding before the runner goes live; demo runs are noise and should not be what gets committed.

title: Typed node verdict contract
description:
Every node returns an enum plus a small payload — never prose. The moment an
edge has to read a paragraph to decide where to go, the router is
nondeterministic again and the state space stops being enumerable.

`./verify` already gets this right: exit 0/1/2 is a three-way typed verdict, and
that is why it works as an edge today. Everything else copies it.

The payload is the other half. If nodes hand each other large prose blobs, this
is a prompt chain wearing a graph costume. The payload should be a small typed
record: issue id, commit sha, file list, evidence path, attempt count.

## Acceptance criteria

- A JSON Schema for the node result envelope.
- Verdict is a closed enum, declared per node type. Reviewer is
  `approve | reject | charter-question`.
- The payload carries what the next edge needs and nothing more.
- A validator that rejects a malformed node result, with a test proving that a
  prose-only result fails rather than being best-effort parsed.
- Documented in GRAPH.md.
close_reason:
Built: nodes/verdict.schema.json (envelope + payload shapes), nodes/node-types.json (closed per-node enums and the edge each verdict selects), bin/cp-verdict (emit | check | schema), tests/test_verdict.py (23 tests).

All acceptance criteria met. The prose-only criterion is satisfied structurally rather than by parsing: a node emits its verdict by calling cp-verdict, so an agent that writes a paragraph leaves no file and there is nothing to best-effort parse. Unknown fields are rejected at emission (the persuasion channel) and stripped again at manifest assembly.

Two additions beyond the original criteria. The question object from the Mastra evaluation landed: a parking verdict must carry the decision being asked, and its options ARE the human node's outgoing edges — so a human node needs no special machinery, and cp brief can render the real question. And the hand-written zero-dependency validator is pinned against the real jsonschema library over a corpus, so the no-install-step premise does not cost correctness.

comments.author: nikital
comments.text:
Borrowed from Mastra's workflow API (evaluated 2026-08-21, not adopted): a suspended step declares a resumeSchema — the shape of the data it needs to continue — separately from the payload it carries.

Apply this to human nodes. A human node should declare the shape of the decision being asked for, not merely park the token. That makes 'cp brief' able to render the actual question and its options rather than 'something needs you'. It is the difference between a decision queue and a notification list, which is the whole thesis of the panel.

So the envelope needs a third piece alongside verdict and payload: for a park-on-human transition, a typed question — what is being asked, what the options are, and what the runner needs back to cross the next edge.

title: verify exit 2 has nowhere to go
description:
The `./verify` contract correctly separates "unrunnable" (exit 2) from "a check
failed" (exit 1), and `bin/verify-all` prints them as different board lines. But
the graph has no destination for 2, so a broken gate would either look like a red
gate or get silently retried. Both are worse than stopping.

## Acceptance criteria

- Exit 2 routes to a human node, distinct from the red-gate repair path.
- A repair node is never handed an exit-2 result to "fix".
- `bin/verify-all`'s "could not be run" wording and the graph agree.
